MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  FEBRUARY 15, 2023

CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee Meeting of the
City of Rolling Hills Estates at 7:02 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, Bacinski, Bain, Chuang, Schachter, Uppal

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Larson, Nicklas (alternate), Schmidt

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Jeannie Naughton, Community Development Director
  Alexa Davis, Assistant City Manager
  Dean Flores, Associate Planner
  Gabby Swain, Administrative Aide
  Carol Corea, Administrative Analyst

3.  INTRODUCTION OF COMMITTEE MEMBERS

CHAIR STEGURA stated that Simone Schmidt was appointed to the Environmental Advisory
Committee at the February 14, 2023 City Council meeting. She thanked the Committee Members
present for their continued service.

4.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING, APRIL 6, 2022

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI
to,
  APPROVE THE ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  APRIL 6, 2022.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

5.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

CHAIR STEGURA noted that a comment was received via email from Brandee Keith with the
South Coast Air Quality Management District (SQAMD) announcing that LA County Supervisor
Holly J. Mitchell has joined the SQAMD’s Governing Board.

6.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A.  RESIDENTIAL FOOD SCRAP/ORGANICS COLLECTION EDUCATION (VERBAL
  REPORT)

CHAIR STEGURA stated that this item is in regard to compliance with SB1383 which went into
effect a year ago; she introduced Erick Quintero with Waste Management who will present this
item.

Erick Quintero, Waste Management stated that he has been working with staff on ideas to drive
compliance with AB1383 and organics in commercial and residential sectors. There has been a
common question about the best utilization for the kitchen food waste pails. He stated that Waste
Management will be sending out their newsletter next month which will include two pages on
frequently asked questions and the usage of kitchen food waste pails. He also noted that there
will be a demonstration on the use of the pails at the city’s upcoming Earth Day event.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN inquired about outreach to the schools and whether this information
will be translated to video content. Mr. Quintero stated that he has been working with staff to
connect with local organizations as well as schools; he also welcomed any contact information
that the committee may have. Mr. Quintero stated that he has been contacting production vendors
for quotes on producing videos that could be used on their website and social media.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, FEBRUARY 15, 2023
 COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL asked about the types of paper that can be used to line the
kitchen pails. Mr. Quintero stated that it would be preferable to use non-coated paper that can
absorb more of the liquid from food waste.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that there is a PV School Gardens and PV Intermediate
School has an environmental club.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that there has been great connection with the schools in the
past; however, now that programs are coming back, staff is looking to reconnect with them. There
have been successful programs with Waste Management in the past, including one teacher who
had a recycling program and some schools have a “no-waste” program.

COMMITTEE MEMBER CHUANG stated that the kitchen pail had a sticker with instructions on
what organics can be disposed in the green waste bins; however, with use and washes the sticker
came off. He inquired if there is a way to add something permanent to the pails. Mr. Quintero
stated that this has been changed to a hot stamp and offered his email to request a new pail.

CHAIR STEGURA asked if there is any data on how the city is doing with compliance. Mr.
Quintero stated that in terms of compliance, the city came in at 49-50% diversion. A lot is being
driven by residential sectors; Waste Management is working on encouraging the commercial
sector on diversion and capturing any data on food donation programs since it can be counted for
the city as diversion and recycling. Mr. Quintero stated that overall the city is doing a great job.

CHAIR STEGURA asked about how the Waste Management newsletter will be distributed. Mr.
Quintero stated that the newsletter will be included with the invoice and will also be available on
the Waste Management’s residential RHE website. Social media graphics are also shared with
staff to share with the residents.

In response to a question by CHAIR STEGURA, Mr. Quintero stated that he welcomes information
on local organizations and events where Waste Management can participate and drive programs
that can improve diversion and provide education to the community.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that Peninsula Seniors puts on several events. She also
asked if containers will be placed at Ernie Howlett and Highridge Park. Also, there is a message
board at Ernie Howlett Park that may be a good place to post information. Mr. Quintero stated
that he and staff have discussed implement placing receptacles at public parks; however, the
challenges are the wildlife and monitoring the usage of the containers.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN suggested that Mr. Quintero get in contact with the sponsors of the
various sports teams who use the parks. She also suggested contacting the HOA’s to include
information in their newsletters.

B.  ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING STATION (EVCS) RATES AT CITY-OWNED
  STATIONS

CHAIR STEGURA stated that staff obtained a grant from SCE to install 6 dual-port Electric Vehicle
Charging Stations (ECVS) at City Hall. This is an addition to the existing ECVS at which the rate
is $0.18 per kilowatt hour. She introduced Gabby Swain to present this item.

Gabby Swain, Administrative Aide, provided a presentation summarizing the staff report and
stated that the current EVCS project at City Hall is near completion and the City should determine
if the established rates should be modified to capture current energy costs. The rates in nearby
cities and the PV Library District were provided, which showed that some systems will add a
charge if a vehicle goes over the specified time limit. The City’s electricity is powered through the
Clean Power Alliance at 100 percent renewable energy.

CHAIR STEGURA added that the City, commercial district and residents are defaulted at 100
percent clean, which is at the higher rate for electricity.

Administrative Aide Swain explained that the cost for electricity that the city is incurring is more
than is being received by EVCS users. Assistant City Manager Davis added that this also does
not include maintenance and software costs. A list of rate options was provided for the committee
to consider.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that the suggestion for the time limit is due to what is currently
happening with the existing stations where people park their vehicles for several hours. As
proposed, once a vehicle is charged, the owner will be alerted and there are stations that will
allow a 20-minute grace period.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  2
 MINUTES, FEBRUARY 15, 2023
 Administrative Aide Swain stated that staff recommends that that the Environmental Advisory
Committee make a recommendation to the City Council on a setting a public usage rate for City-
owned electric vehicle charging stations.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI asked if there is any idea what the usage will be with the new
stations. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that from discussions with SCE, once people are
aware of them, they will become commonly used. The existing ports are used about 90 percent
of the time.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI asked if there is a way to encourage people to move along
once they have reached the charge that they want. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that some
stations will add a charge after a number of hours, others will add the charge immediately when
the vehicle is idle.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that her workplace just increased its rates from $0.18 to
$0.24 per kilowatt hour and is still a reasonable cost. She also added that the time limit is very
important. She stated that when there is a time limit where an additional charge will be added you
pay attention to the time, much like a parking meter. COMMIITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that
either three or four hours would be a good time limit.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SCHACHTER suggested a graduated increase once its idle, after two
hours, a rate of $2.50 per hour and increased from there.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SCHACHTER inquired if the system lets the user know the cost prior to
plugging in. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that the cost can be seen from the direct EV
Connect app or through other apps and maps that will pinpoint that various locations and rates.

CHAIR STEGURA noted that some rate options have a stated time frame, such as 7:00 a.m. –
9:00 p.m. There was a consensus among committee members to remove this; the rates should
be in effect at all hours.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN stated that it’s important to incentivize the use of electric vehicles
considering what the State is doing to move mandatory sales of electric vehicles. She stated that
she is fine with the concept of not making money, but agrees that people need to move on once
their vehicle is charged.

Director Naughton asked about Torrance’s rate structure. Assistant City Manager Davis stated
that Torrance has a rate of $0.33 per kilowatt hour and $0.55 for the first four hours; and $5.00
per hour thereafter.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that $0.24 per kilowatt hour plus $0.50 per session; a 20-minute grace
period; $2.50 per idle hour for the first two hours; and $5.00 per hour thereafter.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SCHACHTER made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
BACINSKI to,

  MAKE A RECOMMENDATION TO SET THE PUBLIC USAGE RATES FOR CITY-
  OWNED ELECTRIC VEHICLE CHARGING STATIONS TO $0.24 PER KILOWATT
  HOUR PLUS $0.50 PER SESSION; A 20-MINUTE GRACE PERIOD; $2.50 PER IDLE
  HOUR FOR THE FIRST TWO HOURS; AND $5.00 PER HOUR THEREAFTER.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

C.  MUNICIPAL CODE UPDATE: SINGLE-USE FOODWARE ACCESSORIES

CHAIR STEGURA stated that this is an extension of a State law that prohibits eating
establishments from handing out a plastic straw unless requested. This new State law applies to
single-use foodware accessories and requires that every municipality adopt an enforcement
mechanism. She introduced Dean Flores, Associate Planner to present this item.

Dean Flores, Associate Planner provided a presentation summarizing the staff report. He stated
that Assembly Bill (AB) 1276 was signed into law in October 2021, which prohibits food
establishments and third-party food platforms from providing single-use foodware accessories or
condiments to customers unless requested. AB 1276 also requires jurisdictions to authorize an
enforcement agency by June 2022. Staff drafted Chapter 8.42 which will be added to the City’s
Health & Safety Code.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  3
 MINUTES, FEBRUARY 15, 2023
 Associate Planner Flores stated that staff recommends that the Environmental Advisory
Committee to review draft RHEMC Chapter 8.42, discuss the issues and provide input and
direction to staff regarding any modifications; provide a recommendation to the City Council
regarding adoption of an ordinance to add Chapter 8.42 (Single-Use Food Accessories) to Title 8
(Health & Safety) of the Rolling Hills Estates Municipal Code.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI asked why public and private school facilities are exempt from
these requirements. Associate Planner Flores stated that there were no explanations for the list
of exemptions.

CHAIR STEGURA asked for further explanation of “complaint-based enforcement”. Associate
Planner Flores stated that the city will not conduct inspections. The City’s Code Compliance
Officer will respond to complaints.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if municipalities are allowed to have standards stricter than
the State level. Director Naughton stated that there is nothing that would prohibit a jurisdiction
from going above and beyond the State’s requirements. One example would be to conduct annual
inspections.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN expressed her concern with complaint-based enforcement since
most of the community would not know that this law is in place. CHAIR STEGURA stated that she
agrees; however, she would not want to make it more difficult for restaurants to do business. She
added that the Chamber will be informed of this new requirement.

COMMITTEE MEMBER SCHACHTER suggested that staff provide letters to all the
restaurants/food establishments. Director Naughton stated that this can be done.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN suggested that the city issue instructions to local restaurants with
the expectations in the community and repeat this periodically; those in compliance be recognized
publicly and businesses not in compliance should be encouraged to do better.

Director Naughton stated that the City does annual restaurant inspection for Heal the Bay
certification; these inspections could be combined The City’s Code Compliance Officer could
provide a courtesy if they are not meeting the requirement. Letters for Health the Bay certifications
are going out tomorrow and language on AB 1276 will be included. In the future, if businesses are
in compliance congratulatory language will be included in the annual Heal the Bay certification
letters.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI
to,
  MAKE A RECOMMENDATION TO THE CITY COUNCIL TO ADOPT AN ORDINANCE
  TO ADD CHAPTER 8.42 (SINGLE-USE FOOD ACCESSORIES) TO TITLE 8 (HEALTH
  & SAFETY) OF THE ROLLING HILLS ESTATES MUNICIPAL CODE. IN ADDITION,
  APPROACH ENFORCEMENT THROUGH AN EDUCATION PROGRAM FOR LOCAL
  RESTAURANTS THAT ENCOURAGES COMPLIANCE RATHER THAN A PUNITIVE
  PROGRAM. ALSO, TO COMBINE INSPECTIONS WITH ANNUAL HEAL THE BAY
  INSPECTIONS AND PROVIDE EDUCATION MATERIALS AS WELL AS DIRECT
  RESTAURANTS TO DISPENSERS FOR SINGLE-USE PLASTICS TO SUPPORT THEM
  IN COMPLIANCE.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

D.  EARTH DAY EVENT (VERBAL)

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that Earth Day will be held on Wednesday, April 19 from
3:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. at the Promenade Mall. Retailers, sustainability, and environmental
partners as well as utility companies will have booths at this event. In addition, the Waste
Management shredding truck will be parked outside of El Pollo Inka. There will also be an
elementary, middle school and high school art contest. Art work will be accepted at the event and
displayed at one of the storefronts. The winners will be recognized at a City Council meeting.
Hopefully, a prize could be donated for the winners.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI stated that years ago he had the Cabrillo Aquarium do a
grunion hatching. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that this would be great and welcomed
contact information be provided to staff.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if the artwork could be displayed at the parks or at the library.
Assistant City Manager Davis stated that this is a great idea.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  4
 MINUTES, FEBRUARY 15, 2023
 7.  MANAGER ITEMS

A.  SOLSMART DESIGNATION AND UPDATE ON SOLAR APP+ (VERBAL REPORT)

Committee Member Bain left the meeting at 8:25 p.m.

Director Naughton provided a presentation on Solar App+. In 2021 the National Renewable
Energy Laboratory (NREL) partnered with experts in building & safety, jurisdictions and the solar
industry to develop plan review software that can run compliance checks and process permits for
rooftop solar systems. In September 2022, Senate Bill 379 became law and requires that most
cities and counties implement an online automating permitting system. Rolling Hills Estates has
a compliance deadline of September 30, 2024. Director Naughton provided an overview how
applications will be submitted and processed. Staff anticipates rolling this out in early March 2023.
Staff applied for and the City was awarded $40K which will be used to make sure that all the
updated codes are uploaded into SolarAPP+. The City contracts with Willdan for Building and
Safety services and the funds will be used to pay them to make sure that all of the updated
information is uploaded to SolarAPP+ and also to pay for staff and Willdan staff training.

Director Naughton stated that SolSmart is a national technical assistance and designation
program and the City can go for a Bronze, Gold and Silver designation. They looks at practices
in permitting and how long it takes to process a permit, as well as any incentive the City may
have. Director Naughton provided an overview of the program and stated that she will provide
these slides to the Committee after the meeting.

CHAIR STEGURA inquired about who would apply for a solar permit. Director Naughton stated
that it would generally be the contractor due to the technical questions that they will be answering.

B.  ITEMS OF INTEREST - NEW FEDERAL ELECTRICAL VEHICLE INCENTIVES (VERBAL
  REPORT)

CHAIR STEGURA stated that she sent an article to staff about the plan under the Inflation
Reduction Act that was passed last year and stated that it may be difficult for some people in the
community to get the incentive for purchasing a new electric vehicle due to income limits. Director
Naughton stated that the tax credit is up to $7,500 and is for the purchase of all-electric, plug-in
hybrid, or fuel cell electric vehicles purchase new before January 1, 2023. There is a link on the
IRS website with more information that will be forwarded to the Committee.

Director Naughton stated that there is an Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit that has
increased after 2022 up to $1,200. The Residential Clean Energy Credit is 30% for qualified
expenditures. There will be a link sent to the Committee to these programs as well as a link to
192 energy efficiency credits/rebates available in California.

CHAIR STEGURA encouraged the committee to send articles, such as these to staff.

8.  COMMITTEE ITEMS/FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS

A.  SUSTAINABILITY ELEMENT FROM GENERAL PLAN

Director Naughton stated that last year, there was discussion on preparing a long-term and a12-
month outlook implementation plan for the sustainability element. She will be bringing this to the
Committee at the next meeting for discussion.

9.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR STEGURA adjourned the meeting at 8:40 p.m.

Submitted by,  Approved by,

_____________________________  ____________________________
Carol Corea, Administrative Analyst  Debby Stegura, Chair

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  5
 MINUTES, FEBRUARY 15, 2023
